tagline.text: Human-faced secondary burial jars from the caves of Maitum, Sarangani

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,500 (mainly transport, per person; check locally)

children.text: Human-faced burial jars found in 1991 by a National Museum team in Ayub Cave, Maitum. These secondary burial jars from the Metal Age about 2,000 years ago are a rare prehistoric heritage in the Philippines and Southeast Asia.

The Maitum jars are earthenware burial jars found in Ayub Cave in Barangay Pinol, Maitum, Sarangani. The cave is now also called Pinol Cave. The jars are secondary burial vessels that hold bones gathered again after the first burial, and a human face and body are modeled into the body and lid, which makes them distinctive as likenesses of particular individuals. Eusebio Dizon of the National Museum, who led the excavation, described the jars as unique finds with no close parallel elsewhere in Southeast Asia.

The story of the discovery begins with treasure hunters. On June 3, 1991, a geologist phoned Dizon to say that people searching for Pacific War treasure had found pottery with human forms, and three days later Dizon received photographs of artifacts that local residents had gathered. Judging the finds important to understanding Philippine prehistory, the team formally began the Maitum Archaeological Project on November 6. Excavation followed in three phases: the first ending in December 1991, the second from April 8 to May 3, 1992, and the third from January 17 to February 15, 1995, and the work recovered 29 burial jars and about 33 baskets (roughly 4 cubic meters) of archaeological material. At the time of excavation, Ayub Cave was described as a Miocene limestone formation about 1 km from the shoreline at an elevation of about 6 m, and Lingling Jabel, the owner of a nearby farm in Pinol, helped with the dig.

Radiocarbon dating puts the jars at about 2,000 years old. Two results from soot on a small pot found inside one of the jars are 1830±60 BP (calibrated AD 70–370) and 1920±50 BP (calibrated 5 BC–AD 225), and the jar culture is classed as the Developed Metal Age, between 190 BC and AD 500. On May 5, 2009 the National Museum declared Pinol Cave an Important Cultural Property, and the jars are also described as national treasures.

For travelers this is a quiet archaeological site rather than a showy attraction. Most of the original jars are kept at the National Museum in Manila, and in Maitum they are known to be encountered through an exhibit on the second floor of the municipal hall and through replicas. Sources disagree on where displays are and whether they are open, so ask the Maitum municipal hall or local tourism staff before you visit. Maitum had about 46,120 people in the 2024 census, the fewest of any municipality in Sarangani, and has 19 barangays, one of which is Pinol. Tarsiers are said to live in the mountains, and the coast has nesting grounds for hawksbill turtles.

The jar heads show expressions from happiness and contentment to sadness and grief. Some faces are full of teeth and others toothless with receding chins and lips, and they are read as portraits that reflect the age and appearance of the deceased. Head size is sometimes read as a sign of age and paint as a sign of status.

Lids fall into four types: a human head, a truncated cone with a simple applied design, a simple oval with four ear-shaped handles, and a truncated cone shaped like an adze with a round spiral motif.

Eyes come in almond, oval, round and rectangular shapes, and eyelids are incised, applied, protruding or flat. Mouths range from one or two rows of incised teeth to open mouths with a visible tongue, and arms and hands are often shown with metal ornaments such as bracelets.

Heads are plain, perforated, or painted red and black with hematite and organic material. The black is read as marking where the hair once was, and some jars were decorated with glass beads and shell spoons and pendants.

blocks.title: Male and female depictions and the difficulty of restoration

children.text: Male breasts are slightly rounded with nipples, while female breasts are shown as gentle bumps without nipples. No complete female jar survives, only many shards of female breasts, which is read as a sign of equality in jar burial.
In 2008, jars and skeletal remains believed to be prehistoric were found in a cave at a quarry on the same mountain, about
from Ayub Cave. The landowner found the cave, and the mayor ordered its entrance sealed until the National Museum could confirm the find.

Ears have a central hole with the upper ear and lobe distinguished, or an oval curling inward with a lobe below. The base of the nose is triangular, concave, beaklike or bulbous. These details are read as evidence that the makers meant to portray individuals.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: Check the exhibit and walk the town

children.text: Travel from General Santos toward Maitum in western Sarangani. No verified source gives the transport or travel time, so ask at the terminal.
In Maitum town, stop at the municipal hall and ask whether the jar exhibit (second floor) and replica displays are open and when.
Look around the exhibit and compare the jars' sizes, expressions and lid shapes using the display panels.
Have lunch locally. Maitum is known for marinated flying fish.
Ask whether Pinol Cave can be visited, but do not enter without permission. The cave is protected cultural property.
Leave Maitum before dark and return to General Santos.

Visiting a cave requires permission from the municipal hall or a local guide. Adjust the schedule to local conditions. Before you see the exhibit, it helps to know that the jars are secondary burial vessels, meaning the body was buried first and the bones were later gathered and placed in the jar, which makes the expressions and decoration far more meaningful. Remember too that this area was affected by conflict in the 1970s, so the site is not fully preserved.
The usual approach is to fly from Manila to General Santos International Airport (GES) and continue overland to western Sarangani. Check the latest flight schedules.
Maitum is in western Sarangani, bordering Sultan Kudarat to the west, Kiamba to the east, South Cotabato to the north and the Celebes Sea to the south.
No verified source gives bus or van routes, fares or travel times from General Santos to Maitum. Ask at the terminal and local information desks.
A modern highway is said to have improved trade and transport.
Between Maitum town and Barangay Pinol, people often use tricycles or motorcycle taxis. Negotiate the fare.
The jar displays are indoors and can be seen year-round, so seasons matter little. Maitum has daytime highs of about
and lows of about
, so it is warm, and it is said to get about 2,696 mm of rain a year over roughly 308 rainy days.
Maitum holds its Binuyugan Festival in May. The festival dates change every year, so check the latest announcements.

News of follow-up research, such as the 2008 Sagel Cave discovery, can be found in announcements from the municipal hall and the National Museum. Cultural heritage sites may be closed to visitors while academic work is under way, so leave your schedule flexible.

Little verified information on lodging is available. The distance and travel time from General Santos to Maitum are also unconfirmed, so check locally whether a day trip is possible. If you want to stay in Maitum, ask the municipal hall first whether there is lodging in town.

Maitum is known for marinated flying fish. With the sea close by, seafood is fresh, but there is no verified information on restaurant names or hours. You can add a visit to a coastal village to the same trip.

In Maitum you can also visit the pawikan (sea turtle) sanctuary, as it is described. The sanctuary was established in 2003, and the Old Poblacion area is known as a nesting ground for hawksbill turtles. If you have time, add a look at the seaside after the exhibit.
Before you go, ask the Maitum municipal hall about exhibit hours and admission rules.
Comparing the jars' facial expressions, eye shapes and lid types makes them easier to understand.
If you want the scholarly context, look for Faces from Maitum by Dizon and Santiago.
Do not touch the exhibits, and check the photography rules.
To visit a cave, always get permission and a local guide.
Ask local residents what these artifacts mean to them and listen respectfully. Maitum is a small town known for the jars as well as its pawikan sanctuary and a May festival.

When a new cave was found in 2008, officials sealed its entrance and advised only photographing and inventorying the site because of looters and treasure hunters. Stay within the area your guide sets.
Pinol Cave and Sagel Cave are protected cultural heritage sites. Entering without permission or touching or removing artifacts is a legal problem.
Most of the original jars are at the National Museum in Manila, and the exhibit in Maitum may be replicas. Adjust your expectations.
Conflict between the military and the MILF in the 1970s caused irreversible damage to the site, and looting and black-market leakage have long been a concern.
Exhibit and cave openings can be irregular. Always check in advance.
Transport information is limited, so allow extra time and confirm your ride back.
Local security conditions can change, so check the latest announcements.
The entrance to Sagel Cave is narrow, about 2.13 m high and 0.76 m wide, and the ceiling is reported to be unstable with loose limestone. Do not enter without permission.
A city with an airport and a transport hub, and the starting point for getting to Maitum.
A highland lake town famous for T'boli culture and the Seven Falls. Reports say Maitum's northernmost village borders Lake Sebu, but plan it as a separate trip.
Described as a sea turtle nesting sanctuary created in 2003. Check locally for its exact location and how to visit.
Maitum's annual festival held in May. Check the latest announcements for the schedule.
